> I would be designing a compact, low-cost digital oscilloscope that uses a microcontroller and a display to visualize low-voltage electrical signals. The device will sample analogue signals, process their readings, and render waveforms on the screen alongside voltage and time-scale information.

## Design

### 2026-10-28: **BOM planning and readme generation**

**2h**

**BOM planning and readme generation**

Before anything started, there is always 2 things that I would like to complete in order to make sure my PCB accommodates those slots and my project matches to my expectations. Hence I went to github, create a repository and spend a very very long amount of time to fill up the BOM, with components that I know I will use, vendors that sell them for cheap in order to fit into the 30usd budget, and the shipping costs when I want to buy them.

Then after generating my entire BOM, took me a whole hour and a half, I went on to creating the readme, allowing people who view my project understand what I'm making, and myself to create a set of objectives that my mini oscilloscope would have to meet. Within this readme, it mentions the features that my oscilloscope would have, project goals that I would like to accomplish, the planned hardware components  (I extracted some from the bom.csv), how the oscilloscope would work and the pictures of my oscilloscope project.

During this time, I also made some sketches of how the oscilloscope design would look like, with M3 screws keeping the PCB afloat and not touching the enclosure, preventing electrical issues, and how the enclosure will support for the screen and USB cables. Just making sure that the entire oscilloscope project would work properly. I'm also really excited to test it out, my very own (and first) oscilloscope ever!!!

### 2026-10-28: **Designing of the entire PCB**

**1.75h**

**Designing of the entire PCB**

This PCB helps to combine every single component together, such as the EC11 rotary encoders, 2 of them one for timebase and the other for voltage, a bornier wire connectors as well, a 1.8inch TFT screen for the waveforms and the graphs that the oscilloscope would produce, and a ESP32 CH340 type c development board as the main microcontroller to ensure that the entire oscilloscope would function properly. I took an extra 30 minutes to work on BOM, finding other vendors, datasheets and all, making sure that the PCB would work properly once it's been made.

[Timelapse](https://lookout.hackclub.com/api/media/2c383581-270d-439a-9431-ca288be5cdbd/video.mp4)

### 2026-10-28: **Firmware coding for the oscilloscope**

**0.75h**

**Firmware coding for the oscilloscope**

In order for the oscilloscope to function, I can't just expect that a few components combined together can do the tasks that it was made to do, hence I went to virtual studio code (VSC) and coded the entire firmware to ensure that the waveforms will be made when voltage is detected and the timebase or voltage rotary encoders are adjusted.

After I coded the entire thing in VSC, I had to go to Arduino IDE and download the ESP32 board tool, and put the entire code into there in order to ensure that I can immediately upload the code into there once the board has been fully finished.

### 2026-10-29: **Completed the entire oscilloscope enclosure**

**1.8h**

**Completed the entire oscilloscope enclosure**

After finishing the entire CAD model for  the oscilloscope, I went on to design an enclosure for it, after all it will be an oscilloscope that I will have to use for a very long time anyways. I designed it with screws so that the electronics components won't touch the bottom of the enclosure and it won't move inside of the CAD enclosure that I made for it, there are dedicated holes for the screen, signal inputs, the microcontroller port, and the 2 rotary encoders.
